title: Testability & Architecture Tests
scopeHtml: Test strategy per layer, test doubles, dispatcher injection, Hilt test setup, screenshot tests, architecture tests (Konsist/ArchUnit-style), boundary enforcement, contract tests, and flaky-test sources that come from architecture choices. Coroutine/Flow mechanics are A1, Compose semantics are A3: cross-reference only.

questions.promptHtml: How would you decide what kind of test to write for each layer of an Android app (UI, ViewModel, use case, repository, data source)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They want to see whether you map each layer to the cheapest test that gives real confidence, instead of "unit test everything with mocks" or "UI tests for everything".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I match the test to what the layer can break. Pure logic, use cases and mappers get plain JVM unit tests. ViewModels get JVM tests with fake repositories and a test dispatcher. Repositories get tests against fake data sources, plus a few integration tests against real Room in-memory or MockWebServer. UI gets Compose tests on stateless screens, a few screenshot tests, and a small number of end-to-end flows. Lots at the bottom, few at the top, and every test runs as low as possible."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A test is cheap when it runs on the JVM with no framework, and expensive when it needs an emulator. Architecture decides how much of your app can be tested cheaply. Google's testing guidance recommends a pyramid-like mix: many small, fast, local tests and fewer large ones.

            /\            E2E / instrumented flows (few, slow, flaky-prone)
           /  \           Compose UI tests, screenshot tests (some)
          /----\          Integration: Room in-memory, MockWebServer (some)
         /------\         ViewModel + repository + use case + mapper unit tests (many, JVM, ms)
Layer Primary test Doubles What it proves
Mapper / validator / reducer JVM unit none pure logic
Use case JVM unit fake repos orchestration rules
ViewModel JVM unit, runTest fake repo, test dispatcher state transitions for given inputs
Repository JVM unit + integration fake data sources; real in-memory Room caching, mapping, error policy
Data source (Retrofit/Room) integration MockWebServer, in-memory DB the SQL/HTTP contract
Composable screen Compose test (Robolectric or device) state passed in as params rendering and click callbacks
Whole app instrumented, hermetic Hilt replaces network wiring and navigation

The rule: test each behavior at the lowest layer that owns it. Retry/backoff policy lives in the repository, so test it there, not through the UI.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Lowest layer that owns the behavior: a pure reducer needs no coroutines at all.
fun reduce(state: CartState, action: CartAction): CartState = when (action) {
    is CartAction.Add -> state.copy(items = state.items + action.item)
    CartAction.Clear -> state.copy(items = emptyList())
}

class CartReducerTest {
    @Test fun add_appendsItem() {
        val result = reduce(CartState(), CartAction.Add(Item("a")))
        assertEquals(listOf(Item("a")), result.items)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing a ViewModel through a UI test because "it is the real behavior": slow, and failures do not point at a layer.
  • Mocking everything so each test restates the implementation; refactors break tests that prove nothing.
  • Chasing one coverage number across layers instead of risk.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you test caching rules? → Repository tests with a fake remote and fake local that count calls and let me control time.
  2. Do you test use cases that just forward to a repository? → Rarely; I would not add a test whose only assertion is a delegate call.
  3. What do you do at the very top? → A handful of hermetic end-to-end flows for login, checkout-type journeys, with network replaced via Hilt.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "unit tests for ViewModels, UI tests for screens." Senior: names the cost and failure signal per level, pushes behavior down to the lowest owning layer, and says what is deliberately not tested.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams with an inverted pyramid (mostly UI tests) end up with CI runs of 40+ minutes and tests people re-run until green.

questions.promptHtml: What makes an Android class easy or hard to unit test? Give concrete examples of code that is hard to test and how you would change it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Testability is a design property. They are checking if you can see the seams (injection points) in a design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A class is easy to test when everything it depends on is passed in through the constructor and it does not reach for statics, singletons, Dispatchers.IO, System.currentTimeMillis() or Context. Hard-to-test code creates its own collaborators or touches the framework. I fix it by extracting an interface at the seam, injecting it, and keeping Android types out of ViewModels and domain code."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A test needs to control inputs (what dependencies return) and observe outputs (state, calls). Every hidden dependency is an input you cannot control.

Typical hidden inputs on Android:

  • Time: System.currentTimeMillis(), Instant.now() -> inject Clock (java.time.Clock) or a () -> Long.
  • Threading: Dispatchers.IO literal, GlobalScope -> inject CoroutineDispatcher or scope.
  • Framework: Context, SharedPreferences, ConnectivityManager -> wrap behind an interface owned by your layer (NetworkMonitor).
  • Static/singleton: Retrofit.Builder() inside a class, object Analytics -> inject an interface.
  • Randomness / UUID: inject a generator.

The seam rule: the interface belongs to the consumer (domain/data), the implementation holds the Android type. Then the class under test has only JVM types.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Hard to test: three hidden inputs (time, thread, singleton).
class TokenManager {
    suspend fun isExpired(): Boolean = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        val exp = AppPrefs.get().expiry
        System.currentTimeMillis() > exp
    }
}

// Testable: all inputs are constructor parameters.
class TokenManager(
    private val store: TokenStore,
    private val clock: Clock,
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
) {
    suspend fun isExpired(): Boolean = withContext(io) {
        clock.millis() > store.expiryMillis()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Injecting Context into a ViewModel "so I can read strings": leaks the Android dependency; expose a UiText and resolve it in the UI.
  • Interface for every class: only add seams where behavior must be controlled or the dependency is slow/non-deterministic.
  • Default parameter hiding the dependency (io = Dispatchers.IO) is fine as a default, but the test must be able to override it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Do you need a DI framework to be testable? → No. Constructor injection is enough; Hilt only helps in tests where you do not construct the object yourself (activities, end-to-end).
  2. How do you test code that must use Context? → Wrap the usage, or use Robolectric for the one adapter class.
  3. What if a library exposes only static/final APIs? → Wrap in a thin adapter I own and test the adapter lightly; do not mock the library.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use Hilt and mock with Mockito." Senior: talks about seams, ownership of the interface, hidden inputs (time, threads, randomness), and that Hilt is orthogonal.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A token-expiry bug around DST/clock changes shipped because the code called System.currentTimeMillis() directly and nobody could write a time-travel test.

questions.promptHtml: Fake, mock, stub, spy, dummy: what is the difference, and which do you prefer on Android and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Over-mocking is the number-one cause of brittle suites. They want to hear a reasoned preference.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A stub returns canned answers, a mock also verifies how it was called, a fake is a working lightweight implementation like an in-memory repository, a spy wraps a real object, a dummy is a placeholder never used. Android's own testing guidance prefers fakes. I use fakes for repositories and data sources, mocks only when the interaction is the behavior, such as 'analytics event was sent once'."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Official Android docs define: Fake = working implementation unsuitable for production (in-memory DB), no mocking framework needed, preferred. Mock = programmed behavior plus expectations, fails if interactions differ. Stub = programmed behavior, no expectations. Spy = real object wrapper tracking calls, usually avoided. Dummy = passed but unused. (Definitions vary by source; Fowler's "Mocks Aren't Stubs" is the reference.)

Why fakes win:

  • State-based assertions ("the list contains X") survive refactors; interaction-based (verify(repo).save(x)) break when you change how you save.
  • A fake can be shared by many tests and by Hilt @TestInstallIn, so one fake serves unit tests and UI tests.
  • Fakes force you to model behavior, which exposes API design problems.

Cost of fakes: you maintain them and they can drift from the real implementation (see contract tests, Q333).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FakeUserRepository : UserRepository {
    private val users = MutableStateFlow<List<User>>(emptyList())
    var failNext: Throwable? = null

    override fun observeUsers(): Flow<List<User>> = users
    override suspend fun add(user: User) {
        failNext?.let { failNext = null; throw it }
        users.update { it + user }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• mockk(relaxed = true) everywhere: a relaxed mock returns defaults silently, so tests pass when behavior is wrong.
  • Verifying private-collaborator calls that are implementation details.
  • Mocking types you do not own (Retrofit service, Room DAO) and then testing the mock; use MockWebServer / in-memory Room.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is a mock the right tool? → When the call is the observable behavior: analytics, a navigation callback, a one-time side effect to an outbound port.
  2. How do you keep a fake honest? → Run the same contract test suite against fake and real (Q333).
  3. Can mockito-style mocks hurt build or run time? → Yes, inline mock maker and reflection add run cost; fakes are plain classes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists definitions. Senior: states state-vs-interaction testing, refactor resilience, shared fakes across unit and UI tests, and fake drift risk with the mitigation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team with 3,000 mock-heavy tests found a 5-line refactor failed 400 tests that had no behavioral change; they migrated repositories to fakes over two quarters.

questions.promptHtml: How do you make coroutine code deterministic in tests? Explain dispatcher injection, runTest, StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher, and what to do about viewModelScope.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most flaky Android unit tests are coroutine scheduling bugs. This checks if you know the mechanism, not just copy-pasted MainDispatcherRule.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I inject dispatchers rather than hardcoding Dispatchers.IO, and in tests I provide TestDispatchers that share one TestCoroutineScheduler. runTest skips delays by using virtual time. StandardTestDispatcher queues new coroutines until I yield, which mimics production and gives control; UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts eagerly, simpler but less faithful. For viewModelScope, which hardcodes Dispatchers.Main, I use Dispatchers.setMain through a JUnit rule."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Facts from the official coroutines testing guide:

  • runTest creates a TestScope whose default dispatcher is StandardTestDispatcher. It does not return while work is queued on its scheduler.
  • New coroutines on a StandardTestDispatcher do not run until the test coroutine yields (advanceUntilIdle(), advanceTimeBy(), runCurrent(), join, or suspension).
  • UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts coroutines eagerly on the current thread but they still suspend at real suspension points such as delay.
  • There must be one scheduler per test. If Main has been replaced with a TestDispatcher, newly created TestDispatchers pick up its scheduler automatically, but only if created after setMain. A TestDispatcher created as a test-class property is initialized before the rule runs and gets its own scheduler: a classic source of "advanceUntilIdle does nothing".
  • runTest timeout default is 60 s (dispatchTimeoutMs as documented in that guide; newer versions use a timeout parameter, verify for your version).
  • If code under test uses withContext(Dispatchers.IO) unreplaced, delays are real and threads race.
 production:   ViewModel -> viewModelScope(Main) -> repo -> withContext(IO)
 test:         ViewModel -> viewModelScope(TestDispatcher via setMain) -> repo(ioDispatcher = same scheduler)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainDispatcherRule(
    val testDispatcher: TestDispatcher = UnconfinedTestDispatcher(),
) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) = Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)
    override fun finished(description: Description) = Dispatchers.resetMain()
}

class SearchRepositoryTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule()
    // Created AFTER the rule property so it reuses the same dispatcher/scheduler.
    private val repo = SearchRepository(FakeApi(), main.testDispatcher)

    @Test fun debounces() = runTest {
        repo.onQuery("a"); repo.onQuery("ab")
        advanceTimeBy(299); assertEquals(0, repo.requests)
        advanceTimeBy(2);   assertEquals(1, repo.requests)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dispatchers.IO default parameter never overridden in the test.
  • Using Unconfined everywhere then missing ordering bugs that production (Main, queued) would hit.
  • launch in a repository's own CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default) with no injection: unreachable from the test.
  • Calling Thread.sleep or delay on a real dispatcher to "wait".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is TestScope.backgroundScope useful? → Collectors of never-ending flows go there so runTest does not hang waiting for them; it is cancelled at test end.
  2. Should you inject Main? → You can for your own code, but viewModelScope hardcodes it, so setMain is still needed.
  3. Why does injecting a scope sometimes beat injecting a dispatcher? → A class that launches its own long-lived work can take a CoroutineScope so the test controls cancellation and lifetime.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "add MainDispatcherRule." Senior: explains the single-scheduler rule, property-initialization ordering trap, and eager vs queued fidelity trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A suite went from a 3% flake rate to ~0 after the team replaced hardcoded Dispatchers.IO in four repositories with an injected @IoDispatcher.

questions.promptHtml: How do you unit test a ViewModel that exposes StateFlow<UiState> built with stateIn(..., SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ...)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: WhileSubscribed is the recommended default, and it makes naive tests hang or see only the initial value. This probes real hands-on testing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "With WhileSubscribed, the upstream only runs while someone collects, so a test that just reads .value sees the initial value. I start a collector in backgroundScope (or use Turbine), drive the fake repository, advance the scheduler, then assert the emitted states. I assert the state sequence that matters, not every intermediate."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
stateIn(scope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) starts the upstream when the first collector arrives and stops 5 s after the last leaves. In a test with no collector, uiState.value is the initialValue forever.

Approach:

  1. Fake repository exposing a MutableStateFlow/MutableSharedFlow you control.
  2. Dispatchers.setMain rule so viewModelScope is controlled.
  3. Collect: backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.uiState.collect {} }, or Turbine's test {} (Turbine version: verify latest).
  4. Emit into the fake; runCurrent() or advanceUntilIdle(); assert vm.uiState.value.

Test the 5,000 ms timeout only if your product logic depends on it (rarely). Using advanceTimeBy(5_001) after cancelling the collector verifies upstream cancellation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FeedViewModelTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule(StandardTestDispatcher())
    private val repo = FakeFeedRepository()

    @Test fun showsItemsAfterLoad() = runTest {
        val vm = FeedViewModel(repo)
        backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.uiState.collect {} }

        assertEquals(FeedUiState.Loading, vm.uiState.value)
        repo.emit(listOf(Item(1)))
        runCurrent()
        assertEquals(FeedUiState.Success(listOf(Item(1))), vm.uiState.value)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Asserting .value immediately after construction and concluding "it loads on init".
  • Collecting with toList() on an infinite flow: hangs until timeout.
  • Verifying intermediate states that conflation (StateFlow) may legitimately drop.
  • Forgetting that a StandardTestDispatcher main requires runCurrent()/advanceUntilIdle() to run init { launch {} }.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not Eagerly in tests only? → That changes the code under test; I want the production sharing policy.
  2. How do you test one-off events? → Collect the event flow in backgroundScope before triggering, since a Channel/SharedFlow with no collector may drop or buffer (see the events chunk).
  3. Where does SavedStateHandle fit? → Construct SavedStateHandle(mapOf("id" to 5)) directly; no Android needed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: copies a Turbine sample. Senior: explains why .value stays at initial, picks backgroundScope, and asserts behavior, not state-emission counts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "passing" ViewModel test never started the upstream, so a mapping bug that crashed on empty lists reached production.

questions.contextHtml:
A 12-person team has a ProfileViewModel test that passes locally and fails about 1 run in 8 on CI (4 vCPU shared runners). Failure: expected:<Success(Ana)> but was:<Loading>. Suite has 1,900 JVM tests, total 6 min. The test and code:

class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: ProfileRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val state: StateFlow<ProfileState> = flow { emit(repo.load()) }
        .map { ProfileState.Success(it) as ProfileState }
        .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProfileState.Loading)
}

class ProfileViewModelTest {
    @Test fun loads() = runTest {
        val vm = ProfileViewModel(FakeProfileRepository("Ana"))
        val job = launch { vm.state.collect {} }
        Thread.sleep(50)
        assertEquals(ProfileState.Success("Ana"), vm.state.value)
        job.cancel()
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every defect, explain why it flakes instead of failing always, and fix both the test and the production code.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the sleep to 200 ms." That hides a real race, slows the suite, and still flakes on a loaded runner. It also misses that viewModelScope needs Main.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it ever fail locally with --parallel test forks? (shows load sensitivity). Is Dispatchers.setMain anywhere in the module? (would explain a different failure). Does the FakeProfileRepository delay? (virtual-time implications).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quarantine with a tracked ticket, do not retry blindly; rerun-on-fail masks the race.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) real Dispatchers.IO via flowOn: the work races the Thread.sleep; (b) no setMain, so viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main, which does not exist on the JVM: it usually throws, but if a test-rule leaks from another class it uses some stale dispatcher; (c) Thread.sleep blocks the single test thread so the launch collector under runTest (StandardTestDispatcher) never even gets to run: collector starts only when the test yields; (d) .value read without waiting.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the single test 200 times (--rerun-tasks with JUnit repeat, or for loop in Gradle) with -Dorg.gradle.workers.max=1 vs 8; add a log of thread names; check for IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize.
  5. Root cause: The test mixes real threads with a test scheduler. Thread.sleep never advances the virtual scheduler, so the collector (queued in the StandardTestDispatcher) has not even started; flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) runs on a real pool. Whether the result arrives before the read depends on timing.
  6. Fix: Inject the dispatcher; use setMain; yield properly.
class ProfileViewModel(
    private val repo: ProfileRepository,
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
) : ViewModel() {
    val state = flow { emit(repo.load()) }
        .map { ProfileState.Success(it) as ProfileState }
        .flowOn(io)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProfileState.Loading)
}

@get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule(StandardTestDispatcher())

@Test fun loads() = runTest {
    val vm = ProfileViewModel(FakeProfileRepository("Ana"), main.testDispatcher)
    backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.state.collect {} }
    runCurrent()
    assertEquals(ProfileState.Success("Ana"), vm.state.value)
}
  1. Prevention: A lint/Konsist rule banning Thread.sleep and Dispatchers.IO/Default literals outside a DispatcherModule; a CI job that runs changed tests 20x to detect new flakes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Not retrying failed tests automatically as the primary fix; it converts a signal into noise. Not switching everything to Unconfined; it can hide ordering bugs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the repo uses Room and the fake is the real DAO? → That is an integration test; use in-memory Room with setQueryExecutor / allowMainThreadQueries or a test executor, and keep it out of the unit suite.
  • What if flowOn is dropped entirely? → Then the repo must be main-safe itself (suspend functions switch their own context); that is the cleaner design and removes the injection from the VM.
  • What if the test must verify the 5 s keep-alive? → Cancel the collector, advanceTimeBy(5_001), assert upstream cancelled via a fake that records cancellation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team had 11 flaky tests all traced to one helper using Dispatchers.Default; fixing the helper's constructor cut CI reruns by roughly 30% and gave back about 90 engineer-minutes a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases sleep, or retries.
  • Hire: identifies real IO dispatcher and sleep, injects dispatcher, uses setMain.
  • Strong hire: also explains why the collector never ran under StandardTestDispatcher, backgroundScope, and adds a repo-wide prevention rule.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test a repository that combines a remote API and a local cache? What do you fake and what do you keep real?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Repositories hold the interesting logic (caching, merging, error policy) and are where over-mocking and under-testing both occur.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I test repository policy with fake data sources I fully control: success, failure, slow, stale. I assert on repository outputs and the fake's state, not on calls. Separately I test each data source against its real technology: DAO with in-memory Room, API service with MockWebServer. That gives fast policy tests and a few slow integration tests that prove the SQL and the HTTP contract."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two different questions, two different test types:

  1. "Given remote fails after cache has data, what does the repository emit?" Policy. Needs fake RemoteDataSource and LocalDataSource. Pure JVM.
  2. "Does my @Query return what I think? Does Retrofit parse this JSON?" Technology. Needs the real thing: Room in-memory DB (Robolectric or instrumented), MockWebServer on JVM.

What to put in the fake:

  • Controllable results: var nextResult: Result<List<Dto>>.
  • Observable state: fun cached(): List<Entity>.
  • Optional gate: a CompletableDeferred so a test can hold the response and observe the loading state in the middle.

Time-dependent policy (TTL): inject a Clock. With runTest's virtual time, advanceTimeBy does not move System.currentTimeMillis(), so a TTL implemented with wall time cannot be tested; use testScheduler.currentTime through a custom Clock or TimeSource.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FakeRemote : ProductRemote {
    var result: Result<List<ProductDto>> = Result.success(emptyList())
    var gate: CompletableDeferred<Unit>? = null
    override suspend fun fetch(): List<ProductDto> {
        gate?.await()
        return result.getOrThrow()
    }
}

@Test fun remoteFailure_keepsCachedData() = runTest {
    val local = FakeLocal(initial = listOf(entity("a")))
    val remote = FakeRemote().apply { result = Result.failure(IOException()) }
    val repo = ProductRepository(remote, local, StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))

    val outcome = repo.refresh()
    assertTrue(outcome is RefreshOutcome.Failed)
    assertEquals(listOf(entity("a")), local.snapshot())   // cache untouched
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mocking Room's Dao interface: tests the mock, not the SQL.
  • Asserting verify(remote).fetch() instead of the observable effect.
  • Not testing the failure path with cached data present, which is where production bugs live.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do mapping bugs get caught? → Mapper unit tests plus repository tests that assert the domain model, not DTOs.
  2. How do you test Flow-returning repositories? → Collect in backgroundScope, emit through the fake, assert emissions at checkpoints.
  3. How do you stop the fake from lying? → Contract tests shared between fake and real (Q333).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: mock Retrofit and DAO. Senior: separates policy from technology tests, fakes with gates and failure injection, uses a clock seam for TTL.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cache-invalidation bug (stale data after a failed refresh wiped the table) escaped because the only test mocked the DAO with a relaxed mock.

questions.promptHtml: How do you set up Hilt for tests? When do you need Hilt in a test at all, and how do you replace a binding?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates either think every test needs Hilt or cannot get an instrumented test to start. They want to see the boundary.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Unit tests do not need Hilt: I call the constructor with fakes. Hilt is for end-to-end and UI tests where the framework creates the objects. There I annotate the test @HiltAndroidTest, add HiltAndroidRule first in rule order, run on HiltTestApplication via a custom runner or Robolectric config, and replace production bindings with @TestInstallIn modules for all tests or @UninstallModules plus a nested module or @BindValue for one test."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the official Hilt testing guide (docs show hilt-android-testing 2.57.1 in the sample; check your version):

  • Dependencies: testImplementation/androidTestImplementation for hilt-android-testing, plus the compiler via kspTest/kspAndroidTest (or kaptTest).
  • @HiltAndroidTest makes Hilt generate a fresh component set per test, so state does not leak between tests.
  • HiltAndroidRule(this) must run before other rules (@get:Rule(order = 0)), or wrap with RuleChain.
  • Application: instrumented tests need a custom AndroidJUnitRunner whose newApplication returns HiltTestApplication; Robolectric uses robolectric.properties or @Config(application = HiltTestApplication::class).
  • Activity host for Compose: an empty @AndroidEntryPoint HiltTestActivity in androidTest (or debug) with createAndroidComposeRule<HiltTestActivity>().
  • Replacing bindings: @TestInstallIn(components = [SingletonComponent::class], replaces = [NetworkModule::class]) applies to all tests in that source set; @UninstallModules per class is more flexible but makes Hilt generate separate components per such class, which the docs warn can hurt build time. @UninstallModules cannot uninstall @TestInstallIn modules.
  • @BindValue binds a field of the test into the graph; @BindValueIntoSet/Map for multibindings.
  • hiltViewModel() composables pick up replaced bindings automatically, since the ViewModel gets its deps from the graph.
 unit test:        new Vm(FakeRepo)                       (no Hilt)
 Compose UI test:  HiltTestApplication -> test graph -> @HiltViewModel Vm(FakeRepo via TestInstallIn)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Module
@TestInstallIn(components = [SingletonComponent::class], replaces = [DataModule::class])
abstract class FakeDataModule {
    @Binds @Singleton
    abstract fun bindRepo(fake: FakeUserRepository): UserRepository
}

@HiltAndroidTest
class ProfileScreenTest {
    @get:Rule(order = 0) val hilt = HiltAndroidRule(this)
    @get:Rule(order = 1) val compose = createAndroidComposeRule<HiltTestActivity>()
    @Inject lateinit var repo: FakeUserRepository   // needs @Inject constructor + @Singleton

    @Before fun setUp() = hilt.inject()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Rule order wrong: "Hilt component not ready" at test start.
  • Fake not @Singleton, so the test's injected instance differs from the one the app uses.
  • Using @UninstallModules in 40 classes and wondering why build time grew.
  • Putting the fake module in main by accident so it ships.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not @TestInstallIn and then change behavior per test? → Make the fake controllable (repo.emit(...)) and share the instance via injection.
  2. Multi-module: where does the test module live? → In the module that owns the tests (app or an androidTest-only test-fixtures module); it can replace modules from dependencies, which is why api/impl bindings must be in @InstallIn modules reachable by tests.
  3. Robolectric or device? → Robolectric for speed and CI; device for real-framework fidelity of a few critical flows.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "add @HiltAndroidTest." Senior: separates unit from Hilt tests, knows rule ordering, singleton identity for fakes, and the build-time cost of @UninstallModules.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's UI suite hit the real staging backend for months because the Hilt replacement module was in a different source set from the one the runner used.

questions.promptHtml: What do screenshot tests buy you, how do Paparazzi, Roborazzi and the Compose Preview Screenshot Testing tool differ, and what makes them flaky or costly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: UI regression strategy at scale. Seniors should say what to snapshot and what not to.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Screenshot tests catch visual regressions that assertion-based UI tests cannot: spacing, theming, truncation, dark mode, font scale. Paparazzi renders on the JVM through LayoutLib with no emulator. Roborazzi runs on Robolectric so it can reach more Android and Hilt integration. Google's Compose Preview Screenshot Testing is built around previews in a separate source set. I snapshot stateless components and screens with fixed state, across a small device/theme/font matrix, and keep the golden images reviewed in PRs."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
What they are: render a composable to a bitmap in a test, compare to a stored golden image with a tolerance; a diff fails the build and the image is part of the PR.

Comparison (from the community comparisons I read; features change fast, so verify against current release notes):

Tool Runs on Notes
Paparazzi JVM, LayoutLib no emulator; its own Gradle task; limited component interaction; not Robolectric
Roborazzi Robolectric runs under the normal unit-test task; can use Hilt; writes diff images; supports Composable Preview Scanner
Compose Preview Screenshot Testing (Google) LayoutLib previews live in a dedicated source set; verify its current maturity

Why they work architecturally: a stateless composable (state in, events out) is a pure function of its parameters, so a screenshot is deterministic. A composable that fetches its own data inside is not. This is the state-hoisting payoff.

Sources of flakiness and cost:

  • Rendering differs across OS/JDK/LayoutLib versions: record and verify on the same CI image, not on dev laptops.
  • Animations, LaunchedEffect delays, network images, current time: freeze the clock, disable animations, use fake image loaders.
  • Golden churn: a design-system tweak can change 400 images; review noise causes rubber-stamping. Keep goldens at component level and a few per screen.
  • Repo size: store goldens with Git LFS or an artifact store if they exceed tens of MB.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Roborazzi-style (APIs: verify against your version)
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
@GraphicsMode(GraphicsMode.Mode.NATIVE)
class PriceTagShotTest {
    @get:Rule val compose = createComposeRule()

    @Test fun lightAndDark() {
        compose.setContent { AppTheme(darkTheme = true) { PriceTag(price = "$12.50", discount = "20% off") } }
        compose.onRoot().captureRoboImage()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Snapshotting stateful screens that hit the network: flaky goldens.
  • Generating goldens on a Mac and verifying on Linux CI.
  • Treating image diffs as approvals without looking.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Screenshot vs semantic assertions? → Semantic tests prove behavior (a click triggers X); screenshots prove appearance. Use both sparingly.
  2. How do you cut the matrix? → Pairwise: light/dark x small/large font x one tablet; not the full cross-product.
  3. Who owns golden updates? → The PR author, with design review on changed images; CI only verifies.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: names a library. Senior: ties it to state hoisting, controls nondeterminism, plans golden review process and storage.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A theming refactor shipped white-on-white text in dark mode on one screen; a single dark-mode golden would have failed the PR.

questions.promptHtml: What is an architecture test, how do tools like Konsist or ArchUnit work, and what rules would you write for an Android codebase?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Architecture erodes through small PRs. Seniors automate the rules instead of relying on review vigilance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "An architecture test is a normal unit test that inspects the code structure instead of running it: it asserts rules like 'domain classes do not import Android', 'ViewModels end with ViewModel and live in presentation', or 'data does not depend on presentation'. Konsist is Kotlin-native and reads Kotlin source, so it understands Kotlin features; ArchUnit works on JVM bytecode. They run in CI like any test and fail the PR that violates the rule."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Konsist (Kotlin source analysis, JUnit/Kotest-based; the docs I read showed version 0.17.3 as current, verify) lets you query Konsist.scopeFromProject(), filter classes/functions/files, and assert. It also has a Layer/assertArchitecture API to declare layers with root packages and who may depend on whom. ArchUnit analyses compiled class files: strong for package and dependency rules, but it sees bytecode, so Kotlin constructs like data class, extension functions or companion objects look different.

Rules worth having:

  1. Layering: domain depends on nothing Android; data depends on domain; presentation depends on domain; nobody depends on app.
  2. Naming/placement: classes extending ViewModel are named *ViewModel, and are internal or in presentation.
  3. No Context/android.* imports in domain and in ViewModels.
  4. No GlobalScope, no Dispatchers.IO literals outside the dispatcher module.
  5. Repositories are interfaces in domain, implementations are internal in data.
  6. No DTO/Entity types in function signatures of public domain APIs.

Within a multi-module project Gradle already forbids dependencies that are not declared, so Konsist rules mostly guard intra-module package structure and conventions.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ArchitectureTest {
    @Test fun domainDoesNotImportAndroid() {
        Konsist.scopeFromProject()
            .files
            .filter { it.packagee?.name?.contains(".domain") == true }
            .assertTrue { file -> file.imports.none { it.name.startsWith("android.") } }
    }

    @Test fun viewModelsAreNamedCorrectly() {
        Konsist.scopeFromProject()
            .classes()
            .withParentNamed("ViewModel")
            .assertTrue { it.name.endsWith("ViewModel") }
    }
}

(API names above follow Konsist docs as I read them; verify exact signatures for your version.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Rules so numerous and strict that people add suppressions: start with 5 high-value rules.
  • Vacuously passing rules on empty scope (see Q331).
  • Testing style (naming of private variables) instead of architecture.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Konsist or Gradle modules? → Modules enforce at compile time with zero tooling; Konsist covers what modules cannot (naming, imports of framework types, package rules inside a module).
  2. Speed? → Parsing a large project's source can take seconds to tens of seconds; run in its own module or only on CI, verify on your repo.
  3. How do you introduce rules to a violating codebase? → Baseline existing violations (allow-list) and fail only on new ones; shrink the list.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "we use ArchUnit." Senior: picks rules by risk, handles baselines, knows module vs test enforcement, avoids vacuous scopes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A domain module slowly acquired androidx imports via convenience; the later KMP extraction cost weeks, which one import rule would have prevented.

questions.contextHtml:
A 40-engineer team added Konsist rules six months ago. Last week a PR added import android.content.Context to GetFeedUseCase in the domain package, and ArchitectureTest was green. Code:

class ArchitectureTest {
    @Test fun domainIsFrameworkFree() {
        Konsist.scopeFromProject()
            .files
            .filter { it.path.contains("/domain/") }
            .assertTrue { f -> f.imports.none { it.name.startsWith("android.") } }
    }
}

Build runs on Windows dev machines and Linux CI. The project has 63 modules, domain sources are at core/domain/src/main/kotlin/com/shop/domain/.... Test takes 11 s.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the test green, how do you prove it, and how do you make it impossible to regress silently?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add another rule for Context." Misses that the rule itself checks nothing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What OS does CI use vs dev machines? (path separator). Is the scope including all modules or only the test module? (scope). When did the test last fail? (never means suspicious).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert or fix the import in the PR; do not wait for the test fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) path.contains("/domain/") fails on Windows \ separators and possibly on how Konsist reports paths; (b) scope narrower than expected; (c) imports of android.* from fully qualified usage (no import) such as android.content.Context written inline; (d) assertion over an empty list passes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Print files.size after the filter; run on both OSes; run a deliberate violation in a scratch class and see the red.
  5. Root cause: In my debugging case the filter yields zero files on one platform, and assertTrue over an empty collection passes vacuously. The test never inspected any file.
  6. Fix:
val domainFiles = Konsist.scopeFromProject().files
    .filter { it.packagee?.name?.startsWith("com.shop.domain") == true }   // package, not path

@Test fun domainScopeIsNotEmpty() = assertTrue(domainFiles.size > 20)      // sanity floor

@Test fun domainIsFrameworkFree() =
    domainFiles.assertTrue { f -> f.imports.none { it.name.startsWith("android.") } }

Then confirm with a canary: a test-only class in the domain package importing android.os.Bundle must make the rule fail (or at least verify the offending file is listed by the assertion message). 7. Prevention: Every architecture rule gets a non-empty-scope guard, filtering by package not path, and a CI check on both OSes; also have the module's Gradle dependencies make domain a pure Kotlin/JVM module so android.* does not even compile. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Not rely only on tests: making domain a kotlin("jvm") module is a stronger guarantee. Not hardcode size == 87, which breaks with every new use case; use a floor.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the import is a typealias in another file? → Imports check fails to see it; the module boundary catches it.
  • What if the rule is correct but slow at 90 s? → Move to a dedicated :konsist-tests module, cache with Gradle, run on PR only.
  • What if teams object to strict rules? → Baseline existing violations and ratchet.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found three of seven architecture rules had zero-file scopes after a package rename; they had been green for a year.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds another rule.
  • Hire: spots the empty-scope vacuous pass and fixes the filter.
  • Strong hire: adds sanity floors, canary violations, cross-OS runs, and makes module type enforce the rule.

questions.promptHtml: You have three ways to enforce architecture boundaries: Gradle module dependencies, custom lint rules, and architecture tests (Konsist/ArchUnit). How do you choose, and how do they layer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand enforcement strength, feedback speed and maintenance cost, not just tool names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I use the strongest cheapest mechanism first. Gradle module graph enforces dependency direction at compile time with no code to maintain, so I split modules where the boundary matters. Custom lint gives IDE-time feedback on API misuse and is good for 'do not call X' rules. Architecture tests catch structural and naming rules inside modules and in CI. They are layers, not alternatives."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism Strength Feedback Cost Best for
Module graph (implementation, api/impl split, internal) cannot compile if violated IDE red + build module/config overhead, build-graph complexity direction of dependencies, hiding impls
Custom lint rules warning/error, inline quick-fix in IDE as you type lint API is awkward, versions break (verify against your AGP) banned APIs, required wrappers, Log.d use
Konsist/ArchUnit tests fail test CI (or locally on run) rule maintenance, runtime of source scan package rules, naming, "domain has no android imports", annotations present
Code review weakest late reviewer attention design intent

Where each shines:

  • "feature-A must not depend on feature-B": module graph. Plus a check that fails if a forbidden project dependency appears (some teams add a Gradle dependency-guard or a graph test).
  • "Never call Dispatchers.IO directly": lint with message pointing to the injected dispatcher, or Konsist.
  • "Every @Entity class is internal to data": Konsist.
  • "Public API of :core:network must not expose OkHttp types": api vs implementation plus Kotlin explicit API mode.

Failure modes of enforcement: rules nobody can fix without exceptions lead to suppression culture; slow rules get disabled; rules without a message explaining why get ignored. Each rule's failure message should say what to do.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts of :feature:checkout:impl  - strongest boundary: it cannot see :feature:profile:impl
dependencies {
    implementation(projects.feature.profile.api)   // allowed
    // implementation(projects.feature.profile.impl)  // not declared -> won't compile
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using tests to enforce what the module graph can enforce for free.
  • Making everything public in Kotlin; internal is free boundary enforcement.
  • No ratchet: turning on a rule that fails 800 places.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not modules for everything? → Each module adds configuration and CI cost; granularity should follow ownership/rate of change.
  2. How do you stop app becoming the dumping ground? → Rule: only wiring in app; test that app contains no business packages.
  3. Lint vs detekt? → detekt rules operate on source via PSI similar to Konsist; lint sees Android semantics/UAST. Choose by what you must analyze, and avoid running three overlapping tools.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "we use ArchUnit." Senior: ranks by strength and feedback loop, uses compiler first, designs rule messages and ratchets.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team relied on code review to stop feature-to-feature imports; 14 cross-feature imports accumulated before modules were split, and each blocked parallel builds.

questions.promptHtml: How do you keep a fake repository honest with the real one, and what are contract tests between modules?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Fakes make tests fast and also create drift risk. Seniors know the mitigation and the module-boundary use.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A contract test is an abstract test suite written against an interface: it states the behavior any implementation must satisfy. I run it against the fake and against the real implementation (with in-memory Room or MockWebServer). If the fake and real diverge, one of them fails. Across modules, the api module can publish the contract suite as test fixtures so every implementer and consumer shares one definition of behavior."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Problem: consumers' tests pass using FakeUserRepository, but the fake returns an empty list where the real one throws NotFoundException. Everything is green; production breaks. The fake encodes your belief about the real thing.

Contract test shape:

abstract class UserRepositoryContract { abstract fun create(): UserRepository; tests... }
  FakeUserRepositoryTest : UserRepositoryContract   (fast, always run)
  RoomUserRepositoryTest : UserRepositoryContract   (in-memory DB)

Items to put in the contract: ordering guarantees, error types for missing/duplicate, behavior of observe after update, idempotency, cancellation safety, null/empty semantics, pagination edges.

Between modules (consumer-driven style): the api module declares the interface; api test fixtures (via java-test-fixtures plugin for JVM/Android library support, verify AGP support for test fixtures in your version) expose the abstract contract and the fake. Feature modules consume testFixtures(project(":data:api")). When behavior changes, you change the contract once.

For network: contract between app and backend is separate (schema checks, recorded responses, OpenAPI/Pact-style tooling, verify applicability); do not confuse with the module contract.

Costs: contract suites take effort to write, and weak contracts give false confidence; they cover what you thought of.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
abstract class NoteRepositoryContract {
    abstract fun repo(): NoteRepository

    @Test fun get_missing_returnsNull() = runTest {
        assertNull(repo().get(id = 404))
    }
    @Test fun add_thenObserve_emitsInInsertionOrder() = runTest {
        val r = repo(); r.add(Note(1, "a")); r.add(Note(2, "b"))
        assertEquals(listOf(1L, 2L), r.observeAll().first().map { it.id })
    }
}

class FakeNoteRepositoryTest : NoteRepositoryContract() { override fun repo() = FakeNoteRepository() }
class RoomNoteRepositoryTest : NoteRepositoryContract() {
    override fun repo() = RoomNoteRepository(inMemoryDb().noteDao())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Contract only on happy paths.
  • Fake that is "smarter" than the real (e.g., auto-generated ids with a different scheme).
  • Letting the fake grow into a second implementation: keep it as small as the contract allows.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is a fake not worth it? → Single-use, trivial dependency: a lambda or stub is fine.
  2. How do you test the server contract? → Recorded fixtures replayed via MockWebServer and a schema validation step in CI; real-environment smoke tests separately.
  3. Who owns the contract in a multi-team repo? → The team owning the api module; consumers add cases via PR.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "write a fake." Senior: names fake drift, shares contract suites via test fixtures, and states limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fake returned Result.success(emptyList()) on offline; the real repository threw, and the offline screen crashed for 2% of users on a flaky-network segment.

questions.contextHtml:
A product team (35 Android engineers, 2,400 JVM tests, 310 instrumented tests, 90 PRs/day). Main-branch CI is red 22% of the time, 4% of individual instrumented tests fail then pass on re-run, and median PR time-to-green is 58 minutes (was 25). Common flaky signals in the log:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize
androidx.compose.ui.test.ComposeTimeoutException: Condition (...) still not satisfied after 3000ms
kotlinx.coroutines.test.UncaughtExceptionsBeforeTest
java.net.UnknownHostException: api-staging.example.com
org.junit.ComparisonFailure: expected:<[2]> but was:<[1]>   (Room query order)

A retry plugin was added "temporarily" four months ago and now retries 3 times.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review. What architecture and test-design causes would you look for, how would you rank and verify them, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more retries and run on better machines." Hides signal, increases cost, and ignores structural causes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do flakes cluster by test class or by runner? (shared state vs infra). Do they correlate with parallel forks? (global singletons). Which tests hit the network? Were flakes rising with a specific change (new retry plugin, new Compose version)? Is test-order randomized?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap retries to 1 and log every retry as a data point; quarantine the top 10 flakiest tests (tag, run in a non-blocking job) and assign owners with a deadline. Do not delete them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) global/singleton state shared between tests (object caches, static Dispatchers.setMain leaks, Dispatchers.resetMain forgotten, Hilt @Singleton fakes not reset when using non-Hilt runner); (b) real dispatchers/time in code (hardcoded Dispatchers.IO, delay, wall-clock); (c) real network or disk (UnknownHost, staging dependency); (d) UI tests with sleeps or no idling sync, animations on; (e) unordered data assumptions (SQL without ORDER BY).
  4. How I'd verify each: Pull flake data from CI (test, runner, duration, retry count) and rank; rerun the top offenders 100x with random order and with parallelism 1 vs N; grep for Thread.sleep, Dispatchers., object singletons, System.currentTimeMillis; check network by running tests with network disabled (sandbox) and see what fails; read UncaughtExceptionsBeforeTest stack for the leaking coroutine's creator.
  5. Root cause: Typically a handful of architectural choices: a global object singleton cache surviving across tests; repositories creating their own CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO); a screen that triggers real work in init; instrumented tests hitting staging; and "wait with delay" instead of idling synchronization. The retry plugin hides each as a coin flip.
  6. Fix: Short term: retries to 1, quarantine lane, kill UnknownHostException by enforcing hermetic tests (Hilt replaces NetworkModule for all instrumented tests via @TestInstallIn). Long term: inject dispatchers/scope/clock; replace singletons with scoped DI instances rebuilt per test; add ORDER BY in queries and in tests; Compose tests use waitUntil/idling or controlled clock, animations disabled (animationsDisabled in test options).
@Rule @JvmField val failOnLeaks = object : TestWatcher() {
    override fun finished(d: Description) { Dispatchers.resetMain() }
}
  1. Prevention: Flake dashboard with a budget (e.g., under 0.5% of runs flaky), flaky tests auto-ticketed to code owner, rule banning Thread.sleep and Dispatchers.IO literals via lint/Konsist, new tests run 20x in CI before merge, test-order randomization on in nightly.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Not ban all instrumented tests: keep a small hermetic set. Not "just rewrite the suite": triage by flake frequency; 20 tests usually cause most of the pain. Not keep retries as policy: retries should be a metric, not a fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the flaky test covers a revenue-critical flow? → Keep it blocking but make it hermetic and deterministic first; add a nightly staging smoke test separately for real-backend coverage.
  • What if flakes only appear on CI emulators? → Compare API level/GPU settings, boot-wait, animation scale; use a managed device farm profile and pin the emulator image.
  • What if product pushes to ship while CI is red? → Gate on the quarantine lane being non-blocking and the blocking set being green; time-boxed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team traced 60% of flakes to one object SessionCache and two repositories with private IO scopes; two weeks of refactoring dropped red-main from 22% to 3%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries and bigger machines.
  • Hire: identifies shared state, real dispatchers/network, quarantine plus ownership.
  • Strong hire: data-driven ranking, hermetic-by-architecture changes, flake budget and prevention rules, rejects retries as policy.

questions.promptHtml: How does your architecture determine how you test Compose screens? Compare testing a stateless screen composable with testing one that obtains its ViewModel internally.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The best UI test strategy is an architecture decision (state hoisting, route/screen split), not a testing-library choice.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I split each destination into a route composable that gets the ViewModel and collects state, and a stateless screen composable that takes UiState and event lambdas. The screen is tested in isolation by passing state and asserting the events, with no DI, on Robolectric or a device. The route is tested by a few Hilt-based tests that prove wiring. That gives fast deterministic UI tests and few expensive ones."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
FeedRoute(viewModel = hiltViewModel())       // wiring: collectAsStateWithLifecycle, navigation callbacks
     └── FeedScreen(state: FeedUiState, onRefresh: () -> Unit, onItemClick: (Id) -> Unit)   // pure UI
  • Stateless screen: input = parameters, output = lambdas. Tests set content with hand-built state (Loading, Error, Success(100 items)), assert nodes, click, verify lambda called. Fast, deterministic, no Hilt, no coroutines.
  • Route: tested with @HiltAndroidTest and replaced bindings; assert that loading a fake repo emission shows the item and a click navigates. Few tests.
  • Compose test rule runs on a test clock; in tests the rule auto-syncs with recomposition and Compose idling, so you rarely need sleeps (mechanics of Compose idling are A3). Use waitUntil for async states.
  • Semantics: prefer onNodeWithText/content descriptions and testTag only where no stable semantic exists.
  • Lazy lists: assert via performScrollToIndex/performScrollToNode; do not rely on off-screen nodes existing.
  • Screen states as previews double as screenshot inputs (Q329).

Design smells that block this: composables calling hiltViewModel() deep in the tree, composables reading singletons, LaunchedEffect triggering network in the leaf UI, UI that depends on Context services.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@get:Rule val compose = createComposeRule()

@Test fun errorState_showsRetry_andInvokesCallback() {
    var retried = 0
    compose.setContent {
        FeedScreen(state = FeedUiState.Error("No network"), onRefresh = { retried++ }, onItemClick = {})
    }
    compose.onNodeWithText("No network").assertIsDisplayed()
    compose.onNodeWithText("Retry").performClick()
    assertEquals(1, retried)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing the route with the real ViewModel for every UI case: slow, and state setup is indirect.
  • Asserting implementation details like exact nesting.
  • Not testing process-recreation behavior with StateRestorationTester where rememberSaveable matters.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Robolectric or emulator for Compose tests? → Robolectric for the bulk (speed, CI cost), emulator for a small set requiring real rendering, input or hardware.
  2. How do you test navigation? → Pass a TestNavHostController and assert the current route; or assert the lambda in the stateless screen; navigation internals are the navigation chunk.
  3. How do you handle animations? → Compose test clock handles most; disable device animations on instrumented runs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use createComposeRule and onNodeWithText." Senior: explains route/screen split, ratio of stateless to wired tests, and the smells that make UI untestable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team with ViewModel-fetching leaf composables could not preview or test them, and their UI suite ran 38 minutes mostly waiting on a real data layer.

questions.contextHtml: Checkout app, 25 engineers, 70 PRs/day. PR pipeline is 47 minutes: 4 min build, 6 min 1,700 JVM tests, 31 min for 260 instrumented UI tests on 3 Firebase-style emulator shards, 6 min lint/detekt. Instrumented tests are billed per device-minute; the finance team asks for a 40% cut in test infrastructure spend. Distribution of tests by what they actually verify (from a sampling audit of 60 tests): 70% of the instrumented tests exercise a single screen's states with the full app and a fake backend; 15% verify navigation; 10% are real end-to-end flows; 5% are visual checks. Flake rate is 2%.
questions.promptHtml: How would you restructure the test suite to hit the cost target without losing confidence?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Delete the slow tests" or "run them nightly only", which removes signal from PRs, or "buy more shards", which raises cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does a regression escape cost (crash rate, revenue)? Which test classes have caught real regressions in the last 6 months? What is the actual device-minute price and billing granularity? Are screens separable into stateless composables already?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shard by historic duration, only run instrumented tests affected by changed modules (module-graph-aware selection), and skip lint on docs-only changes. These reduce cost without removing coverage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) most instrumented tests are testing UI states, which a JVM Compose test can do; (b) app startup per test class with the full Hilt graph dominates the minutes; (c) retries inflate the bill (2% flake x 3 retries); (d) duplicated coverage between nav tests and UI tests.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-test duration and per-class setup time from the test report; count tests by what they assert; the retry histogram; mutation or catch-history to see which tests ever failed for a real reason.
  5. Root cause: The pyramid is inverted: behavior that belongs to a stateless screen is tested through the full app because the screens are not hoisted or the team lacks a cheap harness.
  6. Fix: Move the 70% (182 tests) to Robolectric Compose tests on stateless screens (about 1 s each, runs in the 6-minute JVM stage, parallel forks); keep route-wiring tests for ~20 key screens; keep nav tests as a small set using TestNavHostController on JVM; keep 15-25 real E2E flows on devices; visual checks go to screenshot tests on JVM. Math: 31 minutes x 3 shards = 93 device-minutes now. If instrumented drops from 260 to about 50 tests, estimate ~6 minutes x 3 shards = 18 device-minutes, an ~80% cut; the JVM stage grows by maybe 3-4 minutes on cheap CPU runners. Verify with a measured pilot rather than the estimate.
  7. Prevention: Test-level guidance in the PR template ("lowest layer that owns the behavior"), a CI report of tests per tier, a flake budget, nightly full-suite run for slow safety net.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): Robolectric fidelity is lower than a device (no real GPU/OEM behaviors), so I keep a device smoke set. I would not move E2E tests off PR gating for revenue-critical flows. I would not keep tests I cannot tie to a failure mode.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the screens are not hoisted? → Refactor the top 10 by churn first; the refactor itself pays back in previewability.
  • What if Robolectric native graphics gives rendering differences? → Use it for semantics, not pixel comparisons; use a pinned image for screenshot jobs.
  • What if leadership wants the same cut while doubling features? → Test-impact analysis by module, nightly full runs, and PR-time subset keyed to the changed-module graph.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found that 40% of instrumented minutes were app cold-start per test class; switching to Robolectric for state tests cut PR time from 45 to 19 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes tests or adds shards.
  • Hire: moves tests down the pyramid and shows the math.
  • Strong hire: ties to hoisting, impact-based selection, retry cost, and keeps a device smoke tier with a measured pilot.

questions.contextHtml: A 9-year-old checkout CheckoutActivity (3,100 lines) owns UI, validation, pricing, promo rules and calls to OrderApi via a Kotlin object ApiClient. 1.2M DAU, checkout conversion is the key metric, crash-free sessions 99.2%. There are 0 tests for it. Product wants a new promo-stacking feature in 6 weeks, and the team wants to move to a ViewModel without changing behavior. Previous refactor attempt caused a 3% drop in successful orders for a day (a rounding change in tax calculation).
questions.promptHtml: How do you get this under test and refactor safely, without a big-bang rewrite?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite it with MVVM and write tests after." That is a rewrite with no safety net, repeating the earlier incident.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which logic is highest risk (pricing, taxes, promos)? Is there production data or logs to capture real inputs/outputs? Can I ship behind a flag and roll out by percentage? What is the order success metric alert threshold?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add server-side-comparable monitoring now: order success rate, price-mismatch events, by app version, with a staged rollout and a kill switch for any refactor.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risk is concentrated in pure logic (price, tax, promo math) hidden inside UI code, not in the layout. That logic is easiest to extract and pin with tests first.
  4. How I'd verify each: Instrument and sample real cart inputs and outputs (anonymized), or have QA export 200 representative carts; use coverage reports to see which branches the characterization tests hit.
  5. Root cause: Business rules entangled with Activity lifecycle and a global ApiClient, so nothing can be tested without launching UI.
  6. Fix (strangler, small steps):
    • Step 1, characterization tests: extract pricing/promo functions with "Extract Function" as a pure refactor (IDE-driven, no behavior change), feed them recorded carts, and assert today's outputs, including today's rounding quirks, as golden values.
    • Step 2, introduce seams: wrap ApiClient behind OrderGateway interface; Activity gets it by constructor/factory; real impl delegates to ApiClient.
    • Step 3, move extracted logic into a PricingEngine and a CheckoutViewModel; Activity renders CheckoutUiState.
    • Step 4, parallel run: compute price both by the legacy path and the new engine in production and log mismatches (shadow mode, no user impact). Only switch when mismatch rate is near 0 over a week.
    • Step 5, ship behind a flag, 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, with the order success metric as the abort criterion.
// characterization test: pins CURRENT behavior, bug-compatible
@Test fun legacyRounding_halfUp_perLine() {
    val cart = cartFixture("tax_rounding_case_17.json")
    assertEquals(Money(1_099), PricingEngine.total(cart))
}
  1. Prevention: Golden-file corpus of real carts in CI; rule that business rules live outside Android types; tests added with every bug fix.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not "fix" rounding bugs during the refactor, because a behavior change hidden in a refactor is exactly what caused the earlier incident; fix later as a separate, flagged change. I would not aim for coverage numbers on the Activity itself. I would not block the promo feature: build it in the new engine, so the new code gets tests from day one.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if there is no way to extract without touching UI code? → Start with Compose/Espresso characterization of the end-to-end flow on a few golden carts, then extract under that net.
  • What if shadow mode doubles CPU work? → Sample 5% of sessions and run off the main thread.
  • What if the legacy behavior is wrong? → Decide explicitly with product: preserve (compat) or fix with a flag and comms.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's shadow-run caught a locale-specific decimal-separator mismatch affecting about 0.4% of carts; it never reached users.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rewrite then test.
  • Hire: characterization tests, seams, staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: shadow/parallel run with mismatch metric, bug-compatible golden corpus, separating refactor from behavior fixes, aligned with the product deadline.

questions.contextHtml: A new engineering director announces: "All modules must reach 80% line coverage by end of quarter; PRs below the threshold are blocked." Current coverage is 41% overall. The team has 18 engineers and 62 modules. Two days later a team shows a PR with 200 new tests of the form assertNotNull(Mapper().map(dto)), and a data-class equals test generated for 40 models. The same week, a real bug shipped: cart total off by one cent in locale de-DE, in code with 92% line coverage.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond to the mandate, and what do you propose instead?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either complying and gaming the number, or dismissing coverage entirely without offering an alternative that addresses the director's real goal (quality, fewer escapes).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What outcome is the director after: fewer production defects, faster refactors, audit compliance? Is the 80% for new code or total? Which modules are generated/UI-only? What are the last quarter's top escape causes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the PR block for modules where the gate would force junk tests; propose a trial with a ratchet instead of a fixed target.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The goal is escape reduction, and coverage is a proxy; (b) a hard gate will produce assertion-free or tautological tests (Goodhart's law); (c) the real gaps are in specific risk areas (money, locale, auth, migrations), not uniform lines.
  4. How I'd verify each: Classify last quarter's escaped bugs by module and layer; sample 30 tests for assertion strength; run mutation testing (e.g., PIT via a Gradle plugin; Kotlin support, verify) on 2 critical modules to see whether the 92% covered module's tests catch injected faults.
  5. Root cause: Line coverage measures execution, not verification. The de-DE bug sat in executed lines: no test asserted locale-specific behavior.
  6. Fix (proposal): (i) Coverage of changed lines (diff coverage) at about 70-80% for domain/data logic only, excluding generated code, DI modules, UI glue; (ii) a ratchet: coverage per module must not drop; (iii) risk-based test list for money, locale, time zones, parsing, migrations, with property-style tests for the formatting functions; (iv) mutation score on 2-3 critical modules as a quality signal; (v) track escapes per quarter as the real KPI.
@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(strings = ["de-DE", "en-US", "fr-CH", "ar-EG", "hi-IN"])
fun totalFormatting_roundsToCents(tag: String) {
    val total = formatTotal(Money(1_999), Locale.forLanguageTag(tag))
    assertEquals(1_999, parseTotal(total, Locale.forLanguageTag(tag)).minorUnits)
}
  1. Prevention: Review checklist item: "what bug would this test catch?", test-naming conventions describing behavior, and a monthly review of escapes mapped to missing tests.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not oppose measurement; coverage finds untested areas, and diff coverage keeps new code honest. I would not apply one number to UI, DI and generated code. I would not let the mandate reward test count.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the director insists on the 80% gate? → Agree to the gate on domain/data modules and diff-coverage, with an explicit exclusion list and a review for tautological tests; report escape rate alongside it.
  • What if mutation testing is too slow? → Run it nightly on a few critical modules, or on changed files.
  • What if compliance requires coverage reports? → Produce them (JaCoCo or Kover, verify tool choice) as an artifact without making them the sole gate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite org that gated on total coverage saw 11% of new tests contain no assertion; after switching to diff coverage plus mutation sampling on payment code, escapes in that area fell over two quarters.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: games it or flatly refuses.
  • Hire: explains line coverage vs verification, proposes diff coverage and exclusions.
  • Strong hire: ties to the director's goal, uses escape data and mutation testing, proposes a ratchet and a risk-based test list, and communicates it as a proposal.
